utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Case number IT-95-14/2-T, the Prosecutor versus Dario Kordic and Mario Cerkez.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The first matter to note is that Mr. Kordic is back with us today, having been to the hospital. The next matter which I propose to deal with is the temperature in the courtroom which at the moment seems to be reasonable. Yesterday afternoon, it wasn't, and if it gets hot again, we'll move to another more suitable venue. I shall deal with the submissions which we heard yesterday and give a formal ruling in relation to the matters which are being determined so far. Dealing with the transcript of evidence of Mr. Friis-Pedersen from Blaskic, that, following the decision of the Appeal Chamber in Aleksovski, is admissible, and the Defence have realistically not sought to argue otherwise. Accordingly, the transcript will be admitted, together with the relevant exhibits. In a moment, I will check with Mr. Lopez-Terres to make sure that we have the right exhibits. Let me deal with the other matters, namely, the statement which Mr. Pedersen made to the Prosecutor in August 1996. That will not be admitted at the moment. If the Prosecution wish to have this admitted in addition to the transcript, we shall require further argument upon it. Similarly, the statement of Mr. Haskic will not be admitted for the moment. Again further argument from both parties will be required if that is to be admitted, and at a convenient time we can hear those arguments, if necessary. Mr. Lopez-Terres, I noticed that the transcript has a "Z" number, 2706. Is it proposed that it should be an exhibit in the trial?

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: (Interpretation) That was our intention indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, the exhibits which are attached and which are also, according to Aleksovski, admissible, a report from the Busovaca joint commission to which the witness refers in his evidence, Z754, and it's intended that it should have that exhibit number, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: (Interpretation) That is correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Attached to that is something that was 187A. Is that part of the exhibit? Let me just show you. Just show that to counsel, please. It may be that it's all part of the same exhibit, but I would just like to be sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: (Interpretation) It is indeed the same document, just a part of it having been translated into French.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: [Indiscernible] in the Blaskic trial?

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Exactly, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. The exhibit will be admitted with that number, 754, and the transcript will be 2706. The other matters which were put before us are not admitted at the moment. Can we have the witness back, please? I should have mentioned this, while the witness is coming, that we have to discuss the procedure. I understand that Friday is not convenient for the Defence, and therefore what I propose is that we discuss it at 3.15 tomorrow or thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We discussed the matter amongst ourselves and, subject to the Chamber's ruling, had thought that it might come most conveniently after the next two witnesses. That's today's witness and the one who follows. It had been my hope that those witnesses would be concluded by the end of today and therefore that it might be possible, if the Chamber thought this was a good idea, to launch the procedural matters first thing in the morning. But it's all so uncertain, the timing, that we're entirely in your hands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, after the next two witnesses sounds sensible.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. That helps me with timing the arrival from hotels and so on of the next witness. (Closed session) (The witness entered court).

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: (Open session)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This is Mr. Dzidic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Kadir Dzidic. (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Take a seat. Yes, Mr. Lopez-Terres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Lopez-Terres:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you Mr. Kadir Dzidic, born in 1949?

utterances.speaker: KADIR DJIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the conflict in Vitez, you lived in Vitez, where you were a physics teacher; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KADIR DJIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During your teaching career, one of your pupils was the accused Dario Kordic?

utterances.speaker: KADIR DJIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell the Court, what was your opinion of Dario Kordic as a pupil?

utterances.speaker: KADIR DJIDIC
utterances.text: Yes. He was a pupil who stood out as very industrious, and he applied himself very well to the problems of physics, and he was one of my favourite students.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us if, at the time, Dario Kordic behaved as a person with a rather individualistic character, or did he like to take part in various group activities organised at the time?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: I object. This is clearly leading; probably not particularly relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I agree. Let's go on, shall we?

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: (Interpretation)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us anything else about the behaviour of Dario Kordic, who was your pupil?

utterances.speaker: KADIR DJIDIC
utterances.text: As I said, he was a good student, and disciplined. However, physically, he was not very strong, in order to match the other children at the time, so that sometimes he was slightly pushed aside by those who were more physical and more engaged in physical activities than he was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Dzidic, you still teach physics in a school in Zenica, where you live with your family at the moment?

utterances.speaker: KADIR DJIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Dzidic, is it true that you were a member of the SDA and that you were the president of its local section in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: KADIR DJIDIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were a member of the coordinating committee for the protection of Muslim interests in Vitez; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KADIR DJIDIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Lastly, you were a member of the war presidency in Vitez; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KADIR DJIDIC
utterances.text: I was a co-opted member of the war presidency upon my release from the prison in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you are no longer a member of the SDA, Mr. Dzidic, are you?

utterances.speaker: KADIR DJIDIC
utterances.text: I no longer engage in political activities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Dzidic, for this clarification regarding your work. We shall now move on to those matters of which you have been called to give your testimony here. On 16th April, 1993, around half past 5.00, you were in your flat in Vitez, and you were awakened by an explosion; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KADIR DJIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And from your flat, could you see that some parts of Vitez were under fire or under shelling?

utterances.speaker: KADIR DJIDIC
utterances.text: I saw through the bathroom window that houses in Old Vitez were on fire in the area inhabited exclusively by Muslims. I saw the flash of artillery pieces from Krcevine and Jardol, from where these shells were fired. I saw that the entrances to my building and other buildings had been blocked by people who were my neighbours, some of them in uniforms, and they were all Croats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just a moment, Mr. Dzidic. You are saying that you saw houses ablaze; could you also tell us which were the villages in which, as you saw it, houses were ablaze?

utterances.speaker: KADIR DJIDIC
utterances.text: That was Old Vitez, Stari Vitez, looking from one vantage point. And then, from my own balcony and my neighbour's balcony, I also saw Ahmici on fire. Those were the areas which were -- from where plumes of smoke were rising and where the fires were burning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You tell us that you saw and heard shooting, artillery fire, which came from villages; that is, specifically, the village of Jardol. Was it a Muslim or a Croat village?

utterances.speaker: KADIR DJIDIC
utterances.text: That was a predominantly Croatian village, but there may be a couple of Muslim houses there, too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your view, Mr. Dzidic, the shelling and this shooting that you saw in the morning of the 16th of April, did it come from the HVO, or from the BH army?

utterances.speaker: KADIR DJIDIC
utterances.text: From the side of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You are in no doubt in this regard?

utterances.speaker: KADIR DJIDIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will show you now a document, Mr. Dzidic, which is an aerial view of the town of Vitez. This document was already used, Z2126 (sic). Could we please have this exhibit shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: There is a mistake; it is Z2186, not 2126; 2186. Will you please show this document to the witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Dzidic, can you find your way about that map?

utterances.speaker: KADIR DJIDIC
utterances.text: I'm trying.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please show us where your building was? If, that is, you can find it.

utterances.speaker: KADIR DJIDIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Lopez-Terres, why don't you help the witness with the orientation? Point out some of the buildings.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Could the witness locate the Workers' University building? We spoke about it, for instance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Tell him -- it's difficult for a witness to locate things on an aerial photograph. Tell him where you say it is.

utterances.speaker: KADIR DJIDIC
utterances.text: I think I can find it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Lopez-Terres, will you please tell us where this building is?

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: (Interpretation) You mean the building in which the witness lived? Well, that is precisely what my question was to the witness, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, I want to you explain to us, to start with, where we are supposed to be. The witness doesn't know; we don't know. Now, I've got 2186. What is building "A," please?

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: (Interpretation) I'm really sorry. I was to show the document to the witness. You can retrieve this from me. I'm sorry about this misunderstanding. "A" is Hotel Vitez on this plan. "B" is the cinema building, and we shall come to it later. "C" is the post office building, and "D" is the building which housed the chess club.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Dzidic, do you see where those buildings are?

utterances.speaker: KADIR DJIDIC
utterances.text: This copy is a bit clearer. My apologies, because my eyesight is not that good.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There's no need for you to apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: (Interpretation) We can move on, if the witness cannot give us any information regarding this document today.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Dzidic, your flat was on what floor in that building?

utterances.speaker: KADIR DJIDIC
utterances.text: My apartment was on the fourth floor of the building which is marked with the letter "D."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So your building was in the neighbourhood of the chess club, is it?

utterances.speaker: KADIR DJIDIC
utterances.text: Across from the chess club.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Dzidic. So we were able to locate your building after all. In the morning of the 16th of April, 1993, did you hear -- you told us that there was an attack, and you told us that it was an HVO attack; did you expect that?

utterances.speaker: KADIR DJIDIC
utterances.text: No, I did not expect it in any way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you told us a little while ago that you could see that the soldiers were blocking the entrance into buildings; you also saw soldiers in the street, and at that moment, you decided to go to a neighbour's flat in your building; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KADIR DJIDIC
utterances.text: Yes, I went over to the apartment of my Croatian neighbour. She was a woman with whom I had excellent neighbourly relations. I also took my wife and children with me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You decided to leave your flat because you felt threatened, you felt there was a danger at the moment?

utterances.speaker: KADIR DJIDIC
utterances.text: Yes, that was precisely the reason.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were you afraid of?

utterances.speaker: KADIR DJIDIC
utterances.text: I was afraid of everything that I was seeing. I was afraid that some of the soldiers or someone else would enter my apartment, that something ugly would happen, because something bad could have happened to both me or my wife or my children. This is why I went over to my neighbour. I felt more secure there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And you were, therefore, in your neighbour's flat, and you saw three HVO soldiers arrive; they were wearing camouflage uniforms, and they knocked on the door of your neighbour's flat. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KADIR DJIDIC
utterances.text: The soldiers first knocked on my door, which was across the hallway, a couple of metres away, so I could hear the knocking. It was very loud. Then my neighbour stepped out of her apartment and said that we were not there, that we had gone to Travnik. And then they said that it was not right, that they knew very well that I was in the building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that moment, you, yourself, came out of your neighbour's flat; is that so?

utterances.speaker: KADIR DJIDIC
utterances.text: Yes. I saw that it was an awkward situation. I recognised the men. I invited them into my neighbour's apartment to sit down, have coffee, and talk. They accepted the invitation, came in, sat down. Among them were two men whom I knew by name, and the third one I knew by sight, but I cannot recall his name, even to date. The two whom I knew were Josip Franjic, an ex-student of mine, and Igor Vujica, a neighbour who lived maybe one or two kilometres away from my apartment, whom I had known from some young men who are my relations, and he was associated with them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In addition to these two soldiers whose name you gave us, there was a third person whose name you also mentioned, or rather a part of his name, you gave us?

utterances.speaker: KADIR DJIDIC
utterances.text: Other persons? No, these three soldiers came in. My neighbour and her daughter were present, as well as my family.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember the conduct of the three soldiers? Did they ask for something in particular?

utterances.speaker: KADIR DJIDIC
utterances.text: The third soldier was very nervous. He was playing with his pistol all the time, and he kept asking me where was Fuad Kaknjo, and saying something to the effect that he would kill him as a dog. I was unable to tell him, because I didn't know. After a while, he also calmed down. We all had coffee. Then they left. It was just an informal conversation that we had, and I believe that in the end, we arrived at understanding each other.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who was Fuad Kaknjo?

utterances.speaker: KADIR DJIDIC
utterances.text: At that time, Fuad Kaknjo, and even before the war, he was president of the executive board of the municipality. He was legally elected, and he was very prominent, and he held prominent positions for a period of time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he live in the same neighbourhood as you?

utterances.speaker: KADIR DJIDIC
utterances.text: We lived in the same building. He was in the next segment of the building, the next entrance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. So do you remember still the name of the third soldier? You said there were three soldiers. Do you know the name of the third soldier who was tense and who was asking all those questions about Kaknjo?

utterances.speaker: KADIR DJIDIC
utterances.text: No, I cannot, and I never made it -- I believe that his name was Livancic, but it is not clear to me. I also remembered him as one of my ex-students, but I still cannot recall his first or last names.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned three names, and particularly the name Igor Vujica, and another name, Josip Franjic. I should like to show you two documents, Mr. Dzidic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: (Interpretation) These are documents 2.610 and 2.711, so 2710 and 2711. Would Mr. Usher please help me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Dzidic, you have these two documents before you. The first document -- that is, 2710 -- it is the 19th of May, 1994. It comes from the military authority of Vitez, the Croat Republic of Herceg-Bosna, and you see the name of Igor Vujica, former member of the Vitezovi, who became a member of Vitez (sic) in 1993, on the 15th of December, 1993. Do you see this document relative to Igor Vujica?

utterances.speaker: KADIR DJIDIC
utterances.text: I have this document in front of me, and its heading is "Request for Treatment of a Wounded Soldier in the Republic of Croatia." The registration number is 1779-09/4-09/94-2553.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: KADIR DJIDIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This document, does it relate to the soldier Igor Vujica that you spoke a little while ago?

utterances.speaker: KADIR DJIDIC
utterances.text: Yes, it says 25 March, 1972. I don't know the extent of the injuries of Mr. Vujica and whether he could have been recovered by then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, no, no, I'm referring to the identity. Is that the same person as the one that you spoke about?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Judge, with respect, this is the same kind of examination that we had with the last witness, where this witness is being asked to look at military documents and things of which he should not be familiar and probably is not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He can identify the names on here, but let's move on, because the witness can't say anything more about these, I take it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: (Interpretation)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know the name of the father of Igor Vujica that you told us a little while before in your testimony?

utterances.speaker: KADIR DJIDIC
utterances.text: Yes, this father's name was Nikica, the son's name was Igor, but I don't know about the date of birth. It could be right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You are confirming that the name of the father of soldier Igor Vujica that you spoke about is Nikica?

utterances.speaker: KADIR DJIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The age of Igor Vujica, on the basis of the date of birth indicated in this document, would it correspond, would it tally with the age of Igor Vujica, the soldier that you referred to?

utterances.speaker: KADIR DJIDIC
utterances.text: Yes, it would. It would correspond.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Will you now look at the second document shown here. This is a certificate issued on the 20th of January, 1996, also by the military authority of Vitez, which is issued to an individual called Josip (Nike) Franjic, and it says that on the 16th of April, 1993, he was a member of the Vitez Brigade. The particulars indicated here in this document, would they correspond with the particulars of the soldier Josip Franjic that you spoke about before?

utterances.speaker: KADIR DJIDIC
utterances.text: Yes, they correspond, both the first, last name, and father's name, and again, I cannot say anything about the date of birth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Dzidic. Shall we move on? So you stayed in your building on the 16th of April, and on the 17th of April, that is, the next day, at around 4.00 in the afternoon, soldiers came to your apartment to look for you?

utterances.speaker: KADIR DJIDIC
utterances.text: Yes, they came.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you were taken?

utterances.speaker: KADIR DJIDIC
utterances.text: It was Slaven Kraljevic and another soldier, whose last name I later heard was Krizanac, but I didn't know him then. They took me along. They took me around the building to a cafe called 072, where Darko Kraljevic was located. When they brought me to him, he first said, "Kadir, where is your brother?" My answer was, "Darko, he is on duty, just as you are." Then he asked additional questions, and I responded that if he had anything against my brother or something with him, that he should solve that with him and I was not going to be a go-between. Then he ordered this soldier, Slavko, to take me in a Jeep to the cinema building, and immediately after that we were taken there and I was taken to the basement of the building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you be more exact? Could you tell us who was your brother and what position did he hold?

utterances.speaker: KADIR DJIDIC
utterances.text: My brother is Sefkija Djidic, who at the time was commander of the staff of the Territorial Defence in the Vitez municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us that you were taken to the cinema. At least this is how it is in the French transcript. Is it that you were taken to the cinema building directly or were you first taken to the basement of the building which housed the Workers' University?

utterances.speaker: KADIR DJIDIC
utterances.text: It is the same entrance. The cinema/theatre and the Workers' University shared the same entrance, so I was taken in and then down into the basement.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: (Interpretation) I will now show you two photographs, Mr. Djidic. This document was already produced, admitted, for a previous witness. These documents are from Z2202, and these are the photographs accompanying that document. Please, usher, show this to the witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you please look at all those documents and tell us if they are showing the building that we are talking about?

utterances.speaker: KADIR DJIDIC
utterances.text: The first picture, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Could the witness be shown the second photograph, please?

utterances.speaker: KADIR DJIDIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is also that picture.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: (Interpretation)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next one?

utterances.speaker: KADIR DJIDIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is the building, but a view from another side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can one see the basement in which you were detained?

utterances.speaker: KADIR DJIDIC
utterances.text: You can see the window of the basement here (indicating).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. The next photograph, please. Do you recognise this photograph?

utterances.speaker: KADIR DJIDIC
utterances.text: This is the cinema/theatre which is located in that building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next photograph, please.

utterances.speaker: KADIR DJIDIC
utterances.text: This is another view of the cinema/theatre from a different vantage point.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Djidic. And this photograph, the last one?

utterances.speaker: KADIR DJIDIC
utterances.text: It's the same building and another view from another vantage point.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: KADIR DJIDIC
utterances.text: I think again a different vantage point.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. So these photographs show the building which you call the Workers' University. Others say it's the Workers' House, the Workers' Centre, and other people would call it the cinema?

utterances.speaker: KADIR DJIDIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is the building, because the cinema/theatre was also located or housed in this Workers' University building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. So you told us that you were taken to the basement or to the cellar of the cinema or the Workers' University, and there you found other persons who were already there?

utterances.speaker: KADIR DJIDIC
utterances.text: Yes. There were a number of people there, my Bosniak neighbours. They were all there in this basement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were the people, I mean people who were already in the cellar, were they wearing uniforms?

utterances.speaker: KADIR DJIDIC
utterances.text: Those who were prisoners did not wear uniforms, but those who were guards did wear them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The detainees were the civilians; is that what you are telling us?

utterances.speaker: KADIR DJIDIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they only men?

utterances.speaker: KADIR DJIDIC
utterances.text: These were men of different ages, from 17, 18, up to 65 and above.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After the detention, were perhaps some new detainees brought to the same place?

utterances.speaker: KADIR DJIDIC
utterances.text: This process was ongoing, so the number of people kept rising so that by the night-time, the room could barely hold all the people who were there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there enough room for you in that place?

utterances.speaker: KADIR DJIDIC
utterances.text: No. There was not even enough space to sit down, let alone lie down, and it was also a space which was very badly neglected. There was slag there. It was part of a boiler room. It was where the Workers' University was getting their heat from.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us something about the conditions of detention in that place? How about food, how about hygiene?

utterances.speaker: KADIR DJIDIC
utterances.text: As I said, it was a very cramped space, taking into account all the people who were brought there. As far as food was concerned, nobody even thought about it, but later on we started receiving some food. As far as the hygiene was concerned, it was really substandard. It was also not allowed that we go to the toilet when we needed, so that people had to go to the toilet in a hallway.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How would you define the conditions in the place of your detention?

utterances.speaker: KADIR DJIDIC
utterances.text: Because we had to use this adjacent little room to go and relieve ourselves, the next day there was already this stench coming through, and also there was mud that was brought back into the room in which we were staying, so there was a danger of some disease spreading.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were detained with those other men in this place for several days, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: KADIR DJIDIC
utterances.text: Yes. We stayed there for several days, until the room became too stuffy and too dirty, and then we were able to move to the cinema hall itself, where the sanitary conditions were better, so that the majority of detainees were then transferred there, where we could sit down and get some rest too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Djidic, I will now show you four documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Are you going on to another topic, Mr. Lopez-Terres?

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Well, it still concerns the detention conditions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very quickly, as it's 1.00, and then we will adjourn.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: (Interpretation) These documents are Z767, Z805, Z807, and Z807/1.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Djidic, will you please have a look at these four documents? They are, as you can see, the documents signed by the commander for the HVO forces in Central Bosnia, Colonel Tihomir Blaskic. The first one is dated 21st April 1993. There are two documents on the 24th of April, and the last one is on the 27th of April, 1993. Tihomir Blaskic suggested these documents to the units subordinated to him. The last one on the 27th of April is addressed specifically to the commander of the Vitez Brigade. Can you read these four documents, Mr. Djidic?

utterances.speaker: KADIR DJIDIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did have a look at these four documents. They are fine. But at that time, they were not of much use to us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will ask you, Mr. Djidic, you say these are documents, the orders and calls to obey the request that order be obeyed. Could you tell us, since you were also detained in Vitez during the time at which these orders were issued, could you tell us if you think that these orders, and again invitations to obey orders and reminders of the Geneva Conventions, were they complied with, were they obeyed, at the time when you were detained?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: With respect, I think that's a conclusion only the Court should only draw. More germane, the orders were dated 24 April, 23 April, and, I think, 21 April. The confinement that we've know about thus far is 19 April.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: As far as the dates are concerned, there's no difficulty about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: (Interpretation) But the witness was detained between the 16th and for a time, so at the time when these orders were issued, the witness was still in detention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We'll deal with this after the adjournment. The witness can be asked about the conditions which existed, but can we do it as briefly as possible, because he won't be familiar with these. When you go over the page in the statement, we've had a lot of evidence now about the negotiations involving Dr. Mujezinovic, so those paragraphs could be taken very quickly down to 27.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Very well, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: When we get back, you could briefly ask the witness about these documents and about the conditions in the detention centre. We'll adjourn now. We'll return five minutes later, 25 to 3.00. Mr. Djidic, would you remember, please, during this adjournment and any others, don't speak to anybody about your evidence, and that includes members of the Prosecution. Don't speak about it until it's over. Could you be back, please, at 25 to 3.00. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.05 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lopez-Terres.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: (Interpretation).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Dzidic, before the break, you were shown four documents signed by Colonel Blaskic. You were able to look through those documents, which have to do with the order addressed to brigade commanders regarding the treatment of detainees. Could you tell us whether, during the time you were detained in Vitez, between the 17th of April and the beginning of the month of May 1993, you personally noted a change in the difficult detention conditions that you explained to us this morning.

utterances.speaker: KADIR DJIDIC
utterances.text: I didn't notice any particular change, and having looked through these documents, I see that they were issued with some delay, because the worst things that happened in Vitez were in the first three or four days. As regards the conditions in the prison, they remain more or less the same as they were at the beginning. The prisoners were frequently taken to dig trenches. Sometimes a prisoner would not come back. By way of an example, let me say that Almir Gadjun, a young man in his 20s, was killed during the labour he was taken to do. There were some other cases, but now I'm referring to this particular young man.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm going to show you a document, Mr. Dzidic, which is a death certificate. It is document number 4 among those given to the registrar, with the reference number Z2229. Mr. Dzidic, could you examine this document and tell us whether the person that you referred to as having lost his life while digging trenches is indeed this person whose name appears on this certificate?

utterances.speaker: KADIR DJIDIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Dzidic, during your stay in the detention centre in the Workers' University and the cinema hall, you were chosen to participate in negotiations with representatives of the HVO together with other members of the Muslim community of Vitez. I should like us to refer to those negotiations, and especially the telephone call that you were asked to make. Could you tell us, in connection with those telephone calls, whether you were forced to make them, or whether you had the possibility to refuse to make those telephone calls?

utterances.speaker: KADIR DJIDIC
utterances.text: First of all, like the other participants in the negotiations, we were people from the basement; that is how Mr. Jozic frequently referred to us. People from the basement, as you know, have to be obedient. After these conversations, I was assigned the task to talk to Mr. Ramiz Dugalic, who was the liaison officer of the 3rd Corps of the BH army in Zenica. Until that conversation ended, until the morning, from that conversation until the morning, myself, like the others, had to call anyone we knew in order to stop what they described as the advance of the BH army. I did whatever I could. I understood the gravity of the threat. I realised that all those people held in detention could become victims in that prison, including myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You speak of threats, the seriousness of the threat. Could you specify the nature of that threat? What exactly did you expect before making those telephone calls, or during those telephone calls?

utterances.speaker: KADIR DJIDIC
utterances.text: I expected even murders to take place, because in prison, we heard amongst ourselves that some people had been killed on the first day, in their own apartments, at their thresholds, and in the street. My life was no more valuable than that of those people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You have said that among the HVO representatives with whom you negotiated, there were people whose names you mentioned a moment ago: A gentleman called Bozic, and another person, that is, Mr. Zvonko Cilic. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KADIR DJIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know which HVO units these two persons belonged to?

utterances.speaker: KADIR DJIDIC
utterances.text: I did not know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am now going to show you two documents, Mr. Dzidic, and I'm going to ask you to examine them. They are documents -- Prosecution Exhibits Z703 and Z694. Could you examine the document with the number Z694; it's a document dated the 17th of April, 1993. Do you have it before you?

utterances.speaker: KADIR DJIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us who signed this document?

utterances.speaker: KADIR DJIDIC
utterances.text: Zvonimir Cilic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you also tell us which is the information appearing in the heading? That is, who issued this document? In the top left-hand corner.

utterances.speaker: KADIR DJIDIC
utterances.text: The Croatian Defence Council, the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and then the command of the Vitez Brigade, reference number 02, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. As for the second document, Z703, I hope you have a good copy in the Serbo-Croatian language. It is a document also dated the 17th of April. Could you tell us who signed this document and on behalf of whom?

utterances.speaker: KADIR DJIDIC
utterances.text: It's not legible enough. It says four. I think it says Josic Borislav here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The document in the Serbo-Croatian language is indeed a poor copy, at least the one I have, but in the English-language version, the signature part is far clearer. Could you tell us, in any event, regarding the heading in the left-hand corner, who issued this document?

utterances.speaker: KADIR DJIDIC
utterances.text: The command of the Vitez Brigade, Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I should like to draw to the attention of the Trial Chamber that indeed, the document that I have, in the signature, in the English version, a name appears which is preceded by the name of the accused, and it is much clearer in the English translation than in the Serbo-Croatian version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I don't think we are helped by these documents. I'm going to hand them both back. Hand them in. Let's move on, Mr. Lopez-Terres, please. I'm not admitting those documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: (Interpretation) I thought, Mr. President, that there may be some interest in establishing that the two persons conducting the negotiations belonged to the command of the Vitez Brigade. I shall pass on to the next document, and I shall continue with the examination of the witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Djidic, at the end of the month of April 1993, you were visited by senior representatives of the HVO and the BH army, after which your release occurred. I should like to show you another document, dated the 29th of April, 1993, issued by Colonel Blaskic. It is document Z852. Mr. Djidic, as you are able to see, this document is intended to effect the release of all detainees, particularly civilian detainees, as indicated in paragraph 2 and dated the 29th of April. You explained that you, yourself, and other people were not released then; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KADIR DJIDIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, 13 of us were taken out from the cinema hall in the early hours of the morning and taken to the chess club. The others, I think, were released.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you explain to the Tribunal why, in your opinion, your release and that of the other people did not take effect, in spite of this order?

utterances.speaker: KADIR DJIDIC
utterances.text: I cannot explain that, I never discovered, but when I reviewed the group of people with me, at least ten of them were highly-qualified people who held certain executive posts either in the factory or in the local administration, which was an indication for me that they were detaining people who meant something. I hope this will not sound immodest on my part. People who had a certain standing in town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You have told us that you were transferred to the building of the chess club?

utterances.speaker: KADIR DJIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: (Interpretation) I'm going to show another document, document Z2164. Could this document be shown to the witness? It is the photograph of a building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Djidic, this building, is it the chess club that you mentioned and where you were detained?

utterances.speaker: KADIR DJIDIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is the chess club building. I was detained, I think, here (indicating) in this second section of the building, in the basement of that part of the building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Djidic. You told us that you stayed in this building for several days and then you were transferred to the Kaonik camp, together with other people. During the first days of detention in the Kaonik camp, were you exposed to any threats by the soldiers who were guarding the camp?

utterances.speaker: KADIR DJIDIC
utterances.text: The first two days, there were all kinds of threats that were spoken through the slit in the door. I didn't see who it was, but my impression was whoever passed by the door launched a curse at us, swore at us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you receive any death threats during those days?

utterances.speaker: KADIR DJIDIC
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. There were death threats to the effect, "You will be killed," or, "You will be forced through minefields," and all kinds of things like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. During your detention in the Kaonik camp, you told us that personally you did not suffer any violence, but did you note that other detainees were exposed to physical abuse?

utterances.speaker: KADIR DJIDIC
utterances.text: I was not mistreated in the sense of being beaten. Others, for example, Fuad Kakjno, was taken out and mistreated and, after that, brought back to the prison. Alija Basic was also taken out of the cell. He was threatened, and after all that he didn't feel at all well. As for the others, I cannot say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there, among the detainees in the Kaonik camp, somebody called Smajo Kavazovic?

utterances.speaker: KADIR DJIDIC
utterances.text: There was this person, Smajo Kavazovic, and during a lunch break I saw him eating at a table. We heard of him that he was most probably dead. However, I met him in prison. There were many traces of violence on his face and body.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Around the 15th of May, 1993, you and other detainees of the Kaonik prison were taken to Vitez, taken back to Vitez. Upon your return to Vitez, you met several persons, representatives of the HVO, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: KADIR DJIDIC
utterances.text: I didn't meet them. They came to the hall where we were being detained. Among them was Mario Cerkez, Ivica Santic and Pero Skopljak. They expressed regret should those of us there present decide to leave Vitez, because they offered us every security, assuring us that we should stay, and that Vitez would be the loser if the intellectuals left. However, in view of what had happened before that was not an indication that these people could be trusted, especially so as my family had a day or two previously been expelled in the evening and most of the other people's families had also been driven out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember when, upon your return to Vitez, one of you was hit by a soldier?

utterances.speaker: KADIR DJIDIC
utterances.text: Yes. I think that was the last day that we spent in the cinema hall, when a soldier entered the hall, looking for Suad Salkic. He was carrying a wooden bat, and he beat him with it so that there were traces of blood on his head. The police were present and did nothing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When talking about the police, are you talking about the civilian or the military police?

utterances.speaker: KADIR DJIDIC
utterances.text: I think it was the military police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You and the majority of the other members of the group decided to leave Vitez and to go to Zenica. At the moment of your departure, you were asked to sign a document?

utterances.speaker: KADIR DJIDIC
utterances.text: Yes. We were asked to sign a document saying that we were voluntarily and of our own free will leaving Vitez. I signed it, as did the others.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This document had been prepared in advance, hadn't it?

utterances.speaker: KADIR DJIDIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All you had to do was sign it?

utterances.speaker: KADIR DJIDIC
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: (Interpretation) I have the last document, Mr. President, I should like to show the witness. It is Z2712.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Djidic, will you please look quickly through this document dated the 24th of May, 1993, and entitled, "The Report On The Work Of The Commission To Date"? I should like you to focus in particular on the last part of the first page, where your name appears.

utterances.speaker: KADIR DJIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The names of the persons appearing below yours, does that coincide with the people who were detained with you in Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: KADIR DJIDIC
utterances.text: Yes, but this "Emir Pezer" here who was added to us because he was already in prison when we got there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: KADIR DJIDIC
utterances.text: "Atif Omerovic" is a name I do not know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next paragraph after the list of names that you have just spoken about, there is a report regarding the conditions of the release of a group of 14 people who wished to leave Vitez. You see that paragraph? On page 2, the paragraph after the names. Page 2, at the top.

utterances.speaker: KADIR DJIDIC
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you confirm that this report does indeed relate to the release of you and the others that occurred on the 16th of May, 1993?

utterances.speaker: KADIR DJIDIC
utterances.text: I think that that is the report, because Fehim Beso remained in Vitez; probably Ramo Karajko as well, but I'm not quite sure about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Djidic. Before concluding, Mr. Djidic, I should like to ask you, you left Vitez and you then went to join your family which had been driven out of their apartment, as you have already told us, haven't you?

utterances.speaker: KADIR DJIDIC
utterances.text: Yes. Actually, my family was expelled to Travnik, and I was transferred with the others to Zenica. Then I managed to join up with my family after a period of time in Zenica, because it took time to find accommodation for all of us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you able to take with you any personal belongings when you left Vitez?

utterances.speaker: KADIR DJIDIC
utterances.text: No, I was not able to do that, nor can one carry much going on foot. I tried to get my car back, which was with the police, but I didn't get it. So with a blanket under my arm and some of the things I had in prison, I left and went to Zenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were never able to regain your apartment, were you?

utterances.speaker: KADIR DJIDIC
utterances.text: No, for the present, that is still not possible. I have submitted a request for restoration of my apartment and property. When that will be achieved, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the beginning of your testimony this morning, Mr. Dzidic, you said that you were still a teacher and that you were practising your profession in Zenica. Could you tell us whether today you would have the possibility of practising your profession in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: On relevance grounds, I object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It may not take us very much further, but the witness can answer.

utterances.speaker: KADIR DJIDIC
utterances.text: The school I used to work in, I would probably not be elected a teacher, because as far as I know, there is not a single Bosniak working there with children living in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the programmes, educational programmes, in Vitez are the same as those in the rest of the Federation, the teaching programmes?

utterances.speaker: KADIR DJIDIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, in the Croatian part, the programme is closer or identical to the school programme of the Republic of Croatia. Attempts are being made to agree on a common programme. What the outcome of those negotiations will be, I cannot forecast now.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: (Interpretation) I have no further questions, Mr. President, of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Cross-examination, I hope, in short order, Mr. Stein. Much of this matter has been gone over before.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: I hope you'll be pleasantly surprised. Cross-examined by Mr. Stein:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Dzidic, let me introduce myself. My name is Bob Stein; I represent Dario Kordic. If there's any question that I ask you that you don't understand, let me know. Did you hear my question -- did you hear my statement, sir? If there's any question that I ask you that you don't --

utterances.speaker: KADIR DJIDIC
utterances.text: Yes, I heard you, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, how long have you been a teacher?

utterances.speaker: KADIR DJIDIC
utterances.text: Since 1973.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So roughly 25 years?

utterances.speaker: KADIR DJIDIC
utterances.text: Plus.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you trained to be a teacher?

utterances.speaker: KADIR DJIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it fair to say that the majority of your teaching has been under the communist system that existed in Yugoslavia before the war?

utterances.speaker: KADIR DJIDIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is incontrovertible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do I take it, because you were a teacher, you were addressed as "Professor"?

utterances.speaker: KADIR DJIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if I may, I'll address you as "Professor," if that's all right with you.

utterances.speaker: KADIR DJIDIC
utterances.text: My diploma states that I'm a professor of physics.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very good. Professor Dzidic, let me ask you this: Was there a curriculum for the schools which was imposed throughout the nation of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: KADIR DJIDIC
utterances.text: There was a curriculum for the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that curriculum stressed the communist doctrine; isn't that fair to say?

utterances.speaker: KADIR DJIDIC
utterances.text: Physics does not distinguish between communist or any other doctrines.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I accept that. And having miserable grades in physics, I'll accept whatever you say about it. My question to you, sir, is: You are aware, however, of the rest of the curriculum in the schools; fair enough?

utterances.speaker: KADIR DJIDIC
utterances.text: You know, I taught physics, and my interest in the rest of the curriculum was limited.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let me try it another way: Is it fair to say that under the communist system, the teachings of the communist system required that all people living within the republic be considered brothers and sisters?

utterances.speaker: KADIR DJIDIC
utterances.text: Brotherhood and unity was a slogan which was a guiding thing in the system, and we were taught to take care of each other.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you were taught to be tolerant of each other's religions and ethnic origins as well; correct?

utterances.speaker: KADIR DJIDIC
utterances.text: I was taught in my house to be tolerant of all religions and of all people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And that was also part of the communist doctrine as well, to be tolerant of all religions and all people; correct?

utterances.speaker: KADIR DJIDIC
utterances.text: Well, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in fact, if anyone spoke out against an ethnic group, they would be punished?

utterances.speaker: KADIR DJIDIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were such occurrences.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let me ask you this: Do you know a woman named Emina Kaknjo? And that's E-M-I-N-A K-A-K-N-J-O.

utterances.speaker: KADIR DJIDIC
utterances.text: Emina Kaknjo was a child of Fuad Kaknjo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And she was present when you were interviewed by investigators from the ICTY; correct?

utterances.speaker: KADIR DJIDIC
utterances.text: This person is an interpreter. By coincidence, Fuad Kaknjo has a daughter whose name is Emina; but I believe that the interpreter who was interpreting when I gave the statement happened to have that same name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Fair enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: (Interpretation) If I may, Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: There may be a confusion. There is an interpreter with whom the Prosecutor's office cooperates and whose name is Emina Kaknjo, and to my knowledge, she has nothing to do with Mr. Fuad Kaknjo.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: I accept that; I wanted the mystery cleared up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, let me ask you this question: I want to talk about the meeting that you had, that we've heard so much about, that ended up with Dr. Mujezinovic making a public statement over the television. You were left alone in the office and asked to use the telephone to call some BiH officials to stop the fighting; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KADIR DJIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your current apartment, is that owned -- was that, before you had it, used by a Croat?

utterances.speaker: KADIR DJIDIC
utterances.text: No, it is an apartment of which I was the first occupant, if you're referring to the apartment in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The current apartment where you live.

utterances.speaker: KADIR DJIDIC
utterances.text: The current apartment in Zenica is an apartment where a person lived with his family. He is a mix of Slovene and Croat, and his wife was an ethnic Serb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And last, when you were released, you were exchanged for Croat civilians; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: KADIR DJIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Nothing further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacic? Cross-examined by Mr. Mikulicic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Dzidic. My name is Goran Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: KADIR DJIDIC
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am an attorney from Zagreb, and I represent Mr. Mario Cerkez's Defence in this case. I'm going to ask you several questions, and kindly respond to them to the best of your recollection. Mr. Dzidic, you gave us some personal data; I would just like to clarify a couple of points. Would you please tell us, until the sovereignty of Bosnia-Herzegovina was proclaimed in April of 1992, what was your citizenship?

utterances.speaker: KADIR DJIDIC
utterances.text: Until the proclamation of sovereignty, I was a citizen of SFRY.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And after April 1992?

utterances.speaker: KADIR DJIDIC
utterances.text: I assumed the citizenship of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you assume, or are you sure of it?

utterances.speaker: KADIR DJIDIC
utterances.text: I should be sure of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Dzidic, do you practice your religion?

utterances.speaker: KADIR DJIDIC
utterances.text: Yes. (Trial Chamber confers)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that mean that I can conclude that you regularly go to mosque to pray?

utterances.speaker: KADIR DJIDIC
utterances.text: I go occasionally.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Dzidic, we heard from you that you worked as a teacher in school for a number of years. Given that position of yours, I assume that you knew quite a few people. Would you happen to have known the family of Mario Cerkez, his parents?

utterances.speaker: KADIR DJIDIC
utterances.text: I knew most of the citizens of this small town, at least from passing, and I met and contacted a number of people. I knew the parents of Mr. Cerkez, mostly in a businesslike fashion. They were very polite.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you also have an opportunity to meet Mario Cerkez?

utterances.speaker: KADIR DJIDIC
utterances.text: I think I only met him in passing, and I don't think we ever sat down to have a drink together.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Dzidic, in your contacts with Mario Cerkez's parents, and perhaps superficial contact with Mario Cerkez himself, did you form an impression of that family as a family who had any ethnic or other prejudices?

utterances.speaker: KADIR DJIDIC
utterances.text: No, I could not conclude any such thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Dzidic, you described to us the events, the unfortunate events of 16 April, 1993, when you were awakened by an explosion. Then you went to the apartment of your neighbour, who was an ethnic Croat woman, and there you took shelter, so to speak. Did I conclude that right?

utterances.speaker: KADIR DJIDIC
utterances.text: Yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Am I correct in saying that you actually trusted this woman where you took shelter?

utterances.speaker: KADIR DJIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Dzidic, after that, you said that some soldiers arrived who banged at the door of your apartment, and then you showed them into the apartment of your neighbour, and you recognised two of them. You sat down and had coffee. Mr. Dzidic, can you tell us what type of uniform these soldiers wore?

utterances.speaker: KADIR DJIDIC
utterances.text: Those were camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you perhaps remember, did they have any insignia?

utterances.speaker: KADIR DJIDIC
utterances.text: I think that they had none.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that mean that you cannot tell us to what unit they belonged?

utterances.speaker: KADIR DJIDIC
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Dzidic, you then said that the following day, you were taken to Darko Kraljevic, and of him you said that he was the commander of Vitezovi? That's how you said it?

utterances.speaker: KADIR DJIDIC
utterances.text: No, I did not say that he was the commander of Vitezovi, but it is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So he was a commander of Vitezovi?

utterances.speaker: KADIR DJIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you were taken to a coffee bar?

utterances.speaker: KADIR DJIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall the name of that place?

utterances.speaker: KADIR DJIDIC
utterances.text: It is called 072. It is right below my apartment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Given the proximity of it, could you tell us whether this place was some kind of a headquarters of the unit commanded by Darko Kraljevic?

utterances.speaker: KADIR DJIDIC
utterances.text: I cannot say, because I never entered it. Darko Kraljevic was in front of it, where there were some tables where guests would sit. That's where I met him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Dzidic, does this part of town where you lived have a name, Kolonija?

utterances.speaker: KADIR DJIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Dzidic, where is the coffee bar called "Benz"?

utterances.speaker: KADIR DJIDIC
utterances.text: Next to that bar in the neighbourhood.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mean next to this 072 coffee bar?

utterances.speaker: KADIR DJIDIC
utterances.text: They're either one next to another or very close by one another.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that these two coffee bars share an outside terrace, a garden?

utterances.speaker: KADIR DJIDIC
utterances.text: No, I cannot tell you because I never went there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Djidic, you said that Darko Kraljevic had ordered you arrested and taken to the cinema/theatre; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KADIR DJIDIC
utterances.text: No, I said that he said that I should be taken to the cinema building when I was arrested.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To whom did he say this?

utterances.speaker: KADIR DJIDIC
utterances.text: It was to his brother, Slaven, and another man. I believe his name was Krizanac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But would I be wrong in saying that these two soldiers were of the unit commanded by Darko Kraljevic?

utterances.speaker: KADIR DJIDIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure, but they may have been.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Djidic, you talked to us about conditions in the basement where you were placed, and then you said that you were invited to make certain telephone calls. I believe we're referring now to 19 April 1993. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KADIR DJIDIC
utterances.text: I cannot specify the date, but I was made part of the team which was to conduct negotiations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question was about the telephone calls to the BH army commanders.

utterances.speaker: KADIR DJIDIC
utterances.text: Yes. After the conversation with the HVO officials, I was given a task of talking to the liaison officer of the 3rd Corps of the BH army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I must ask you again, because I'm not sure that I understood it right. Were you in any way forced to make those telephone calls or was it suggested to you?

utterances.speaker: KADIR DJIDIC
utterances.text: A moment ago I mentioned that we were the people from the basement, and this was often pointed out during this time, which also meant that, "You better be quite careful if you want to see your family survive."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On 18th of April, 1993, a cessation of all hostilities was arranged between the leadership at the very top, that is, the HVO and the BH army?

utterances.speaker: KADIR DJIDIC
utterances.text: I was not familiar with the outcome of these negotiations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But did you hear something about it?

utterances.speaker: KADIR DJIDIC
utterances.text: Later on, but not at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever think that in a situation where a day before a cease-fire had been negotiated, arranged, that you would be invited to have it implemented?

utterances.speaker: KADIR DJIDIC
utterances.text: I did not know about it, but my overall opinion was that all this should come to an end.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, that is clear. But, Mr. Djidic, who, in that first building where you first found yourself, took you to the chess club?

utterances.speaker: KADIR DJIDIC
utterances.text: There were soldiers in a van.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were these members of the military police?

utterances.speaker: KADIR DJIDIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't know. They were in uniforms. I don't know whether they were policemen or officers or what.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But do you know who took you from the chess club to Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: KADIR DJIDIC
utterances.text: They were also soldiers, and I believe that the driver was civilian.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know members of which military units were guards in Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: KADIR DJIDIC
utterances.text: No. How could I know that?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you don't know anything about members of these units?

utterances.speaker: KADIR DJIDIC
utterances.text: I was on the other side of the door.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Djidic, while you were in the cellar, as you put it, could you ask and get medical assistance?

utterances.speaker: KADIR DJIDIC
utterances.text: At that time, I did not need any, even though I already had papers to go to the hospital. But only a few days later, a physician arrived, and he told me that I didn't, after all, need to go to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember who that doctor was?

utterances.speaker: KADIR DJIDIC
utterances.text: Dr. Franjo Tibolt.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he examine you on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: KADIR DJIDIC
utterances.text: No. We only talked.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During that time, were you made to engage in some manual labour?

utterances.speaker: KADIR DJIDIC
utterances.text: No, I was spared the trench digging.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who spared you? Who gave you the paper sparing you from that?

utterances.speaker: KADIR DJIDIC
utterances.text: Dr. Franjo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Djidic, at the time of your release you said you had to sign a statement. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: KADIR DJIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will now show you a document. Will you please try to identify it and tell us if that is the statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Will the usher please take care of these documents?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document is marked D28/2.

utterances.speaker: KADIR DJIDIC
utterances.text: This is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you tell us the number under which your signature figures?

utterances.speaker: KADIR DJIDIC
utterances.text: Number 13.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Thank you. Usher, you can take those documents, you can collect those documents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember, Mr. Djidic, at the time when you were released with other people, did the television make a record of this and were there journalists present there?

utterances.speaker: KADIR DJIDIC
utterances.text: There was a television crew there, as far as I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Thank you very much, Mr. Djidic. I have no more questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Any questions?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We're sorry, we could not hear the Prosecutor. The microphone was switched off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Djidic, thank you for coming to the International Tribunal to give your evidence. It is now concluded, and you are released.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Your Honours, before the next witness is called in, I should like -- (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Thank you, Your Honours. I shall be very brief. During the examination of an earlier witness, I believe it was Dr. Mujezinovic offered a photocopy of a document. Now we have the original of that same document, and I should like to tender it into evidence for authenticity. It was 20/2, that is, D20/2. So will the usher please take this document from me? I have it for him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, as you know from this morning, I was expecting to move to procedural matters after this witness and therefore didn't bring another witness here for the afternoon. I understand that the Defence aren't in a position to go ahead with the procedural matter because Mr. Smith isn't here, which is unfortunate. I haven't been served in advance with any notice of what their position is going to be, but they've only had since yesterday to look at the statement, although they've had over a week, I think, to look at the dossier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It seems to me that it's very unfortunate to waste even 20 minutes of time if we can use it to good purpose. Before I return to the subject of the dossier, the Court may recall, may have before it, or may indeed, want to remind itself of my printed arguments for procedural possibilities at some stage before the argument is advanced by the Defence, because the pressure of time on the last occasion we visited this problem, or not problem, this issue, was such that I had to take you through it very quickly. It's probably not with you on the bench at the moment, but I would ask that you obtain the opportunity, if you find it helpful, to consider it or reconsider it before starting again on this issue. It's probably helpful if I just also set the scene for procedure. It's been a long time coming because we've always put the taking of evidence ahead of everything else, and very sensibly, if I may respectfully say so. But right at the beginning, the Chamber raised the issue of the witness list, not on the basis that it was going to make any cuts at that stage or anything of the like, because it said specifically just because of its wanting to know what the position was. I then set out our position, subject to further procedural developments, and although it was a matter between -- effectively, it's a matter between the Bench and the Prosecutor, each defendant had an argument on, or was allowed an argument on, the witness list generally at that stage, and subject to my reply, that was really an end of it. What happened then was that I raised specifically the issue of the dossier in my procedural paper as one solution to the problem, and it's obviously not inappropriate that the Defence should be allowed to discuss that in general terms in the same way as if I sought to call the witness, they would be able to object to the witness being called. That's, I think, the way things stands at the moment. Outstanding procedural matters, apart from the dossier, include, I suppose, timetable matters arising from the modest change to the timetable of the availability of seven more half days. I had set out in my paper, and I'll remind you of this, that as to experts, I had hoped to be able to serve you with two more of the total of four intended expert reports of a general nature by the end of this week, and I hope that's still going to be possible. I then invited the Court to consider the possibility of reading those expert reports between the end of this week and the next sitting of this Chamber in order that we could take the experts really very swiftly. I had raised as a possibility a practice that saves time in certain jurisdictions and is wholly unobjectionable, so far as I'm concerned, which is that competing experts, experts from opposing sides, can not only be called back to back, if that's a course acceptable to all, but that indeed the experts can be put together outside court, before they ever come to give evidence, so that they can narrow the issues that exist between experts on one side and another. I have no doubt that those who have tried any form of conventional case involving expert witnesses will know how long expert evidence can take if it is all explored in detail in court, how all too frequently when that's done --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Mr. Nice, you are saying that several experts could be together. Not too general, but let us take a case, for instance, an expert opinion about an area or about a town. Would that be within the framework of your proposal regarding the dossier? Is this related to the presentation of the dossier or is it a proposal which goes over and above the question of dossier, because this would be within the context of the dossier, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This, Your Honours, is entirely separate from the dossier I mentioned in my procedural paper. It relates to experts who are experts in particular fields, and so that in this case we have historians and we intend to have a constitutional expert in matters of that sort, and those are the experts I had in mind. I think experience does show that if you take experts who are experts in a narrow field, coming to a court to give evidence on a narrow range of topics, time can frequently be saved by them being invited to consider the extent to which they truly disagree and the extent to which they agree. I've raised this in my paper. I haven't had any response yet from the Defence. I don't know what their attitude to it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I don't have your paper in front of me. There's one aspect of it that I recall had to do with the question of cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You quoted the relevant provision of International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, which speaks of the right to examine and to have examined. Thereafter, you, I think, pointed to a commentary on it, and I think you are suggesting that that comment made the point that the formulation that I have referred to is the way it is to take account of differences in the two legal systems or in different legal systems. What I wanted to find out from you is whether you are suggesting that the right to examine and have examined witnesses as a right of the accused, whether the International Covenant is satisfied in some systems without the accused actually having the right to cross-examine. I don't know whether that is the point that you are getting at, that the right to examine and have examined does not necessarily mean, in some legal systems, that the witnesses have to be cross-examined by the accused person.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour's recollection of the detail of the paper is very accurate. It's certainly the case using the word "witness" in the way which Your Honour does, that some systems do not demand or require that the defendant should have the right to cross-examine the witness when the word "witness" is used in that way. May I respectfully submit that, first of all, this Tribunal itself, in its general acceptance of hearsay, of course acknowledges that the defendant doesn't have the right to cross-examine everyone who, as it were, might be able to give evidence against him or her, and may I suggest that one of the interesting issues that this problem throws up is the real difference between the two systems, the common law and the civil system, and it shows the difficulties that practitioners on one side or the other have with dealing with the other system's approach to evidence. It's probably a good idea, if I can presume so to say, to use the word "witness" only in respect to people who come to court or, alternatively, who give evidence by video link, and to find and uniformly to use another word for people whose evidence would be given through that witness. Sometimes, I think, in the jurisprudence with which we are familiar, when looking at the famous common-law concept of hearsay, wholly unknown to the civil lawyers, the word "declarant" is used, the declarant of a statement.
