One could use that word. One could use the word "observer" for somebody who observes events, whose observations are then transmitted to the Court through the witness who brings them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Can I just interrupt you: I'm not too concerned, overly concerned about the jurisprudence of the Tribunal, which I know, and which obviously, if it comes from a certain body, is binding; but I would be very much helped in my appreciation of the entire problem that we are looking at if I could be persuaded that the International Covenant, which I consider the basic human rights document, certainly next to the Universal Declaration, if it could be shown to me that that instrument legitimises or authorises a situation in which an accused person does not necessarily have a right to cross-examine a witness, but that that witness -- or declarant or maker or provider of information; it doesn't matter to me what you call that person -- but that person is examined or -- in some other way, you know? My concern is to satisfy myself that the norms in the Covenant, which, in my view, reflect customary international law, are satisfied in that kind of situation. And I wondered -- my thoughts were provoked when I saw the comment in your paper that I think the Covenant was formulated in the way it was to meet the variations, the vicissitudes in different legal systems.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, my understanding of the question is that the answer is yes. To some extent, the answer is particularised by the examples we give from the civil system, as understood by us, and proposed. It's helpful to have your question overnight. I will attempt, if I may, to bring further chapter and verse to show that such systems fall within the Covenant for you first thing in the morning, if that would help. But it's certainly the case, under the civil systems that we have summarised -- and they're not all the same -- that witnesses bring information from declarants or observers, and that there is no automatic right to have each and every observer or declarant -- absent some particular exception: death, or whatever -- there is no absolute right to have those people brought before a court, although in certain of the jurisdictions, as we understand it, there is a strong presumption that important ones will, of course, be made available. But it appears, for example, in the French system -- and Mr. Lopez-Terres will correct me if I'm wrong, or probably Judge Bennouna -- but in the French system, the Court decides the degree to which the defendant's case requires that there should be witnesses available for cross-examination, assuming the witnesses are available, but nevertheless is free to draw on other material, providing that material is read out, so that it's part of the public record, for its final decision. And that must accommodate the Covenant and must fit within it. But if you can give me until tomorrow morning, now that your question is completely articulated, I'll hope to be able to bring you some more specific answers to that problem. Certainly, if we aren't able to fit such practices within the Covenant, then there's the general policy of the Tribunal, and its approach to hearsay would present a difficulty. But that's for another day, maybe, because that issue is clearly resolved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, moving on, you mentioned experts and a suggestion about experts.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, has there been any discussion between the parties about this suggestion?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I haven't heard back from the Defence on that. Before I close what I have to say about experts, there's the outstanding issue of the constitutional expert. Just to remind the Chamber, the constitutional expert we originally hoped to be able to call gave evidence and was extensively cross-examined in Blaskic. Well before the trial, I summarised, in a digestible way, his evidence, served it for admission, but it was rejected. That witness, in light of what happened to him after he gave evidence in Blaskic, is not prepared to come in person to help us, and we are attempting -- I think we have identified a substitute expert. It's plainly a witness that has to come, not least because of the very detailed account given of constitutional matters in the Defence pre-trial brief, which, although not identified as to its author, would appear to be the content of an expert's report. One of our problems in identifying a substitute expert has been the hope that the Prosecution's case will finish within a reasonably short period of time. Therefore, if an expert is available but only available next year, we've had to rule him out. I think we have now identified an expert, but I'm not sure how long it's going to take me to have the report prepared for service. That apart, there will be three, I think, by the end of this week or the very beginning of next week. You've seen one of them already. The second one comes from Mr. Cigar and the third from Mr. Allcock. I'm anxious that their testimony can be taken in the most concise and useful way possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: But unless there's agreement by the Defence on this matter, you'll have to call them in the conventional way.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, of course. I accept that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Your suggestion would be that the experts should meet, or something of that sort, or should correspond, and try and thrash out what is in dispute and what is agreed between them?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, because it's a practice that in other areas works very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It seems a sensible suggestion and limits the amount of evidence. The time which is necessary given to it can be given to it outside. Well, we'll put that matter to the Defence in due course. Looking ahead, since we've got another five minutes, as I've said, we have to fix the calendar for the rest of the year. I'm sorry that hasn't been done already, but it's because of the difficulties of other cases impinging on this one. I do recognise that for those involved, it does cause an inconvenience if you don't know what you're supposed to be doing in the autumn, so we shall come to it as soon as we possibly can. I think it likely -- although it's not yet decided -- that we shall be sitting from the 13th of September. To start with, I shall be engaged in another case in the morning, for some of that time, and we shall run through until October. We hope fairly soon to be able to give you some finalised dates. What I think would be helpful, from the point of view of the Trial Chamber, from the Prosecution, is an estimate of how long they are going to be, because we may want to take a view about that. How long is it going to take for the rest of the Prosecution case? Given, for instance, if you had full court time, how long would it take for you to finish your case, having in mind, for instance, how long Blaskic took?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As you know, I have always hoped that our case, although similar in overall scale of issues to Blaskic, would take a very substantially shorter period of time, not least because we have the advantage of being able to learn lessons from what's happened in Blaskic. My belief is that if the dossier approach finds favour -- and if it's something that we can accomplish, because it's very labour-intensive on our side, I have to say, but if it's acceptable, we'll find the resources to do it -- then that will immediately save a very considerable amount of time. My further belief is that the techniques that I've been developing for taking evidence in chief are paying off, I think quite handsomely, in the time that evidence is taking, not only because evidence in chief is getting shorter, but it seems to me that there is a corresponding focus by the Defence that is shortening cross-examination. I would like a day or so to look, with my team, at the witness list, with those various possibilities in mind, and in a sense, I'd be helped by knowing what the response to the dossier issue is, although that may take some time to come from the Chamber; I recognise that. But I would think that if you give us a couple of days, I can give you, one way or another, some target periods of time that I estimate our case will take. I have to say that there are always going to be odd problems along the way. We are, for example, encountering some difficulty with witnesses generally, rather more than we'd expected, including in respect of witnesses who were very recently willing. That always creates difficulties for us because we've got to decide what our response to their attitude is, and our response may itself be sometimes time-consuming, or it may be simply the response of choosing other witnesses, and so on. So there are always going to be unexpected or developing difficulties, but I think things are in hand, and within a few days I could give you an estimate of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Tomorrow, you propose, Mr. Nice, hearing one witness; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No, the Defence have indicated an hour and a half, I think, for the procedural discussion. I have no idea of the time it may take; I will obviously require -- or may need to say things in reply. But if it's an hour and a half out of the morning, that would take us till -- well, I would hope not only to do one witness, but two witnesses, by Friday lunchtime, is the short --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Why is it suggested that the procedural matters should take precedence tomorrow morning over the evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Only because, if you remember, this morning, you had suggested procedure tomorrow afternoon, and I had suggested that we take procedure because it had been partially agreed after Dzidic, and you said that was satisfactory. I'm quite happy to start a witness, or Mr. Scott's quite happy to start a witness at 9.45 tomorrow morning and to take him as swiftly as may be, and that will then leave a witness, perhaps, for Friday, who I would hope could be taken in -- completely, start to finish -- in the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, we'd better resolve this procedural matter tomorrow morning first thing, one way or another. Mr. Stein, can I address you on behalf of the Defence, in the absence of Mr. Smith?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It may be that one approach to this problem of the dossier is having seen it -- and we'll hear your objections, although I think we can probably anticipate them -- one approach may be to test the system, as it were, further, with one dossier, and see how that works or doesn't work in practice. I don't expect a response to that now, but that may be a suggestion which is made tomorrow. I can tell you, thinking aloud, myself -- this is a purely personal opinion about it -- there is in the dossier a great deal of material which, under our Rules, is potentially admissible; that would be the documentary material and the photographs and the like. That leaves the issue of the witness statements, which I suppose is the nub of the matter, and about that there can be argument. But one approach might be, your having had the summary, is to ask you what's in dispute here, what is the real issue about this village, and then determine what, if any, witnesses should be called on that issue. I put that forward for your consideration, and we'll hear your submissions on it tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: I won't preclude those or preview them now, except to say that I believe sincerely that the dossier approach will lengthen and not shorten this trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Mr. Stein, what has been proposed by the Court is an experiment; it is not a question of faith and what we believe in. We should rather like to go into juridic science and experiment a little. It is not a question of what we believe in or not. That will not help us to make progress. This being so, if we pass from the area of beliefs to the area of science and practice and experimentation, we all have in mind the rights of the accused, the rights of the Defence. I think that is essential, and that is the reply to what was said a moment ago by my colleague, Judge Robinson, about the Covenant on Civil Rights. That is the respect of the rights of the Defence. There are different ways of respecting the rights of the Defence, but it is essential that those rights be respected. If we go through this dossier and you tell us that for such-and-such a person mentioned, or statement mentioned, we need to hear them, then there will be no problem; but as for others, there is no reason to bring them, because they will be repeating what other people have said. There may be witnesses who will be repetitive. In that case, we will be economising, all of us, and that is the spirit in which we are working. Respect for the rights of the Defence: Nothing should be done that would infringe upon that right. But on the other hand, we must respect the institution, not to waste time and resources without any cause. And I think, with a certain degree of an open mind, we may go ahead with this kind of an experiment, and that is the spirit that I wish to convey to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Judge, perhaps it's because I'm a New Englander; I have a reputation for being conservative. But in fact we have many experiments going on in our jurisdiction. I have tried civil cases in which we've put on our damage evidence before we got to our liability evidence. I've tried cases to summary juries, where you make an offer of proof of your case, and they give you an opinion. We have many novel experiments. I must confess the idea of duelling experts in the back room, while I've heard it before, just intrigues me intellectually, but I'm not sure we're going to agree to that in this particular instance. So it's not that we're afraid to make innovative techniques, and I'm sure the Chamber, as do we, weigh the balance of that innovative technique to not only the search for truth, but the defendants' rights as established under our process. Mr. Smith will address that, as only he can, and I will address it, hopefully, tomorrow, on a more practical level -- having put my foot in it, I'll just leave it there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, if you could have the witness here at a reasonable hour tomorrow, I hope we won't be too long with this argument.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We'll have him here straight away, first thing in the morning, I think, for safety.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Can we know who the witness is?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: One of them is seeking some protection. I'll tell my friends the order I propose to take them, unless they've got any objection. If not, it's the next two witnesses on the list, because the last three I cancelled, as they will remember. The only other evidence that I might seek to lead this week, if time allows, is the two witnesses who took the statement from Dr. Mujezinovic which has been the subject of such heavy complaint.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And to the extent we can have their summaries ahead of time, it certainly is helpful.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, that's not a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Tomorrow morning at quarter to 10.00, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
